Champion

CHAM-pee-uhn · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To champion is to actively support or advocate for a cause.

Senator Ruiz has championed clean-water legislation for over a decade.

Worked Example

Though she never sought credit, the retired nurse championed the free clinic at every town meeting, petition drive, and budget hearing.

She actively and publicly supported the clinic's cause, again and again, in front of others -- that ongoing public advocacy is what it means to champion something.

How Strong Is It? — support → champion → crusade

support vs. champion

support vs. champion: To support a cause can be as quiet as signing a petition -- to champion it means stepping out front and fighting for it publicly.

crusade vs. champion

crusade vs. champion: To crusade for something is even more intense than championing it -- a relentless, almost single-minded campaign.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — champ

Root — champ: field; battlefield (from Latin campus, 'field,' which became champ in French)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: one who (via Late Latin campio, 'fighter in the field')

Put it together

Put it together: Champ ('field,' from Latin campus, 'battlefield,' which turned into champ in French) + -ion ('one who,' via Late Latin campio, 'fighter in the field') — a champion is the fighter who takes the field on someone's behalf. So to champion a cause is to step onto the field and fight for it.

Use the root in a new word: campaign

Use the root in a new word: campaign: The students ran a recycling campaign that placed labeled bins in every hallway.

Root Check

Word Choice

On this card, champion is a VERB: you champion a cause, a bill, or a reform -- you fight publicly for it. English also uses champion as a noun for a contest winner, but that is a different sense: when you see 'championed reform,' think advocacy, not trophies.
